analysis.one_liner: Sets up a voluntary national label for genetically engineered foods and bars states from requiring disclosure.
analysis.headline: The Senate Agriculture Committee reported the bill and put it on the calendar the day it was introduced, but the Senate never voted on it before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have the Department of Agriculture create a national labeling standard for genetically engineered ("bioengineered") foods — but companies would only label if they chose to. It would also block any state or local government from requiring genetically engineered food or seed to be labeled. State laws like Vermont's, which was set to take mandatory labeling in 2016, would be wiped out. The bill never came to a Senate vote; it died on the calendar when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Packaged-food makers and agricultural biotechnology companies. A single voluntary national standard replaces a patchwork of state labeling mandates, so companies decide for themselves whether to disclose genetic engineering, and no state can force them to. It also orders USDA to run education and outreach promoting the benefits of agricultural biotechnology [S2][S3][S4].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Food makers and biotech seed companies

how_it_helps.text: Requires USDA to set up a national labeling standard for bioengineered foods within two years, but the standard is voluntary — a food may be labeled 'bioengineered' only under USDA rules, and no company is required to label at all [S2][S3][S4].
Preempts state and local laws: no state may require labeling of genetically engineered food or seed for foods in interstate commerce, unless identical to the federal voluntary standard [S2][S3][S4].

Bars regulations that would let anyone claim a food is safer or higher quality based on whether it is bioengineered, and orders USDA to provide 'science-based information' promoting consumer acceptance of agricultural biotechnology [S2][S3][S4].

analysis.who_pays: Consumers who want to know whether their food contains genetically engineered ingredients, and state governments. States that passed mandatory labeling laws would lose that authority, and under a purely voluntary standard most genetically engineered foods could reach shelves with no disclosure at all.
analysis.who_pays_short: Consumers seeking ingredient disclosure, and state governments

drawbacks.text: Because the standard is voluntary, companies that do not want to disclose genetic engineering simply would not label, leaving consumers with less information than state laws would have required [S2][S3].
The bill preempts every state and local labeling requirement for genetically engineered food and seed, voiding laws like Vermont's that were scheduled to take effect in 2016 [S2][S3][S4].

USDA is directed to run education, outreach, and promotion of the benefits of agricultural biotechnology, putting the agency that writes the labeling rules in the position of advocating for the industry being labeled [S2][S3][S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is built around food-industry concerns: one national standard instead of 50 state rules, and no mandatory disclosure anywhere. The benefit to consumers is essentially the option to label; the cost is the loss of state laws that would have required disclosure. For anyone who wanted mandatory GMO labels, this bill was the opposite of what they sought — opponents dubbed it the 'DARK Act.'

outcome.mechanism: Senator Roberts reported it out of the Agriculture Committee and placed it on the Senate calendar the same day it was introduced, but the Senate never voted on it, and it died on the calendar when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced on March 1, 2016, and reported the same day as an original measure from the Senate Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry Committee chaired by Senator Roberts, then placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders [S6].
The bill would create a national voluntary labeling standard for bioengineered foods and preempt state and local genetically engineered food and seed labeling requirements [S2][S3].

No floor vote ever occurred in the record: the next and last action was the committee's written report filed December 9, 2016, and the 114th Congress ended January 3, 2017 with the bill still on the calendar [S6].
The bill had zero cosponsors, and the Senate record shows no vote on the bill itself [S5][S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: In the immediate term, states and consumer-labeling advocates kept their laws alive because the bill died. But the underlying fight ended a month later, when Congress passed a related compromise requiring some form of disclosure (including electronic QR codes) that still preempted stricter state laws — so packaged-food and biotech companies ultimately got the nationwide regime they wanted, just in a different bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Food makers, via a later compromise

for.name: Sen. Pat Roberts
for.role: Chair, Senate Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill as a committee original measure, reported it to the Senate, and placed it on the Senate calendar on the day of introduction; later filed the committee's written report.

for.name: Senate Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry Committee
for.what_they_did: Reported the original bill to the Senate without a written report on March 1, 2016; filed written report No. 114-403 in December 2016.

for.name: Packaged food and grocery industry coalition
for.what_they_did: Publicly backed a national voluntary standard and federal preemption of state GMO labeling laws over a patchwork of state mandates.

against.name: Consumer and food-labeling advocacy groups
against.what_they_did: Campaigned against the bill as the 'DARK Act,' arguing a voluntary standard with state preemption would deny consumers the labeling that state laws had mandated.

against.name: Sen. Patrick Leahy
against.what_they_did: Opposed federal preemption of state GMO labeling laws, including Vermont's mandatory labeling law set to take effect July 1, 2016.

against.name: State of Vermont
against.role: State with a mandatory GMO labeling law (Act 120)
against.what_they_did: Its labeling law, scheduled to take effect July 1, 2016, was the principal law this bill would have preempted, making it the focal point of opposition to preemption.

sides.party_line_note: The record contains no roll-call vote on this bill, so no party breakdown exists; contemporaneous reporting showed Republicans backing the voluntary approach while most Democrats backed mandatory labeling.

industries.note: A single voluntary national standard would end state-by-state mandatory labeling, saving compliance costs while giving consumers no guaranteed disclosure. The industry's gain came directly at the cost of state labeling laws consumers had won.

The bill preempts state labeling of genetically engineered seeds as well as food, and bars claims linking bioengineering to safety or quality, while ordering USDA to promote acceptance of biotechnology. It protects markets for engineered crops against state-mandated disclosure.

Organic and voluntary non-GMO certification programs would continue, and a voluntary standard does not restrict voluntary 'non-GMO' claims by the Secretary's determination; these marketers had catered to consumers who wanted disclosure.
